texts.title: Two Poems by Christina Rossetti
texts.author: Christina Rossetti
texts.source: Both poems are from Sing-Song: A Nursery Rhyme Book by Christina Rossetti, first published in 1872. The poems have no titles in the book, so each is known by its first line. Text from the 1893 Macmillan edition (Project Gutenberg eBook #76703), checked against the 1907 Macmillan edition. Public domain in the UK.
lines: Who has seen the wind?
Who has seen the wind?
Neither I nor you:
But when the leaves hang trembling
The wind is passing thro’.
Who has seen the wind?
Neither you nor I:
But when the trees bow down their heads
The wind is passing by.
What is pink?
What is pink? a rose is pink
By the fountain’s brink.
What is red? a poppy’s red
In its barley bed.
What is blue? the sky is blue
Where the clouds float thro’.
What is white? a swan is white
Sailing in the light.
What is yellow? pears are yellow,
Rich and ripe and mellow.
What is green? the grass is green,
With small flowers between.
What is violet? clouds are violet
In the summer twilight.
What is orange? why, an orange,
Just an orange!
glossary: an old short way of writing through
a crop, like wheat, grown in fields
the dim light just after the sun sets

texts.title: The Story of the Three Little Pigs
texts.author: Joseph Jacobs (collector)
texts.source: From English Fairy Tales (1890), collected by Joseph Jacobs: the start of the tale, without its opening rhyme. Project Gutenberg eBook #7439. Public domain in the UK.
lines: There was an old sow with three little pigs, and as she had not enough to keep them,
she sent them out to seek their fortune. The first that went off met a man with a
bundle of straw, and said to him:
“Please, man, give me that straw to build me a house.”
Which the man did, and the little pig built a house with it. Presently came along a
wolf, and knocked at the door, and said:
“Little pig, little pig, let me come in.”
To which the pig answered:
“No, no, by the hair of my chiny chin chin.”
The wolf then answered to that:
“Then I’ll huff, and I’ll puff, and I’ll blow your house in.”
So he huffed, and he puffed, and he blew his house in, and ate up the little pig.
The second little pig met a man with a bundle of furze, and said:
“Please, man, give me that furze to build a house.”
Which the man did, and the pig built his house. Then along came the wolf, and said:
“Little pig, little pig, let me come in.”
“No, no, by the hair of my chiny chin chin.”
“Then I’ll puff, and I’ll huff, and I’ll blow your house in.”
So he huffed, and he puffed, and he puffed, and he huffed, and at last he blew the
house down, and he ate up the little pig.
The third little pig met a man with a load of bricks, and said:
“Please, man, give me those bricks to build a house with.”
So the man gave him the bricks, and he built his house with them. So the wolf came,
as he did to the other little pigs, and said:
“Little pig, little pig, let me come in.”
“No, no, by the hair of my chiny chin chin.”
“Then I’ll huff, and I’ll puff, and I’ll blow your house in.”
Well, he huffed, and he puffed, and he huffed and he puffed, and he puffed and huffed;
but he could not get the house down. When he found that he could not, with all his
huffing and puffing, blow the house down, he said:
“Little pig, I know where there is a nice field of turnips.”
glossary: go off to make a new life
a prickly wild bush, also called gorse
a playful way of saying chin

texts.title: Grow a Bean in a Jar
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Original text. Method checked against Science and Plants for Schools (saps.org.uk) and Science Sparks (science-sparks.com).
lines: A bean is a seed. Plant it in soil and everything happens out of sight. Plant it in a jar and you can watch it start to grow.
You will need
1 broad bean seed
a clean glass jar
kitchen paper
a cup of water
What will happen?
After about 4 days, the seed coat cracks and a root pokes out. The root grows downwards. It holds the plant steady and finds water and nutrients.
Next, a shoot appears. The shoot grows upwards, towards the light.
What to do
1. Soak the bean in the cup of water for 1 hour.
2. Fold 2 sheets of kitchen paper. Wet them, then squeeze them so they are damp but not dripping.
3. Wrap the damp paper round the inside of the jar.
4. Push the bean down between the paper and the glass, about halfway up, where you can see it.
5. Stand the jar somewhere light, such as a windowsill.
6. Check the paper every day. If it feels dry, add a little water.
Top tip
Keep a bean diary. Each day, draw your bean and write the date underneath.
glossary: the tough outer skin of a seed
the things a plant needs from soil to grow healthy

texts.title: The Tale of Peter Rabbit
texts.author: Beatrix Potter
texts.source: From The Tale of Peter Rabbit by Beatrix Potter, first published in 1902. The extract leaves out the opening line that names the rabbits, and stops part-way through. Project Gutenberg eBook #14838. Public domain in the UK.
lines: They lived with their Mother in a sand-bank, underneath the root of a very big
fir-tree.
‘Now my dears,’ said old Mrs. Rabbit one morning, ‘you may go into the fields
or down the lane, but don’t go into Mr. McGregor’s garden: your Father had an
accident there; he was put in a pie by Mrs. McGregor.’
‘Now run along, and don’t get into mischief. I am going out.’
Then old Mrs. Rabbit took a basket and her umbrella, and went through the
wood to the baker’s. She bought a loaf of brown bread and five currant buns.
Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cottontail, who were good little bunnies, went down the
lane to gather blackberries:
But Peter, who was very naughty, ran straight away to Mr. McGregor’s garden,
and squeezed under the gate!
First he ate some lettuces and some French beans; and then he ate some
radishes;
And then, feeling rather sick, he went to look for some parsley.
But round the end of a cucumber frame, whom should he meet but Mr.
McGregor!
Mr. McGregor was on his hands and knees planting out young cabbages, but
he jumped up and ran after Peter, waving a rake and calling out, ‘Stop thief!’
Peter was most dreadfully frightened; he rushed all over the garden, for he
had forgotten the way back to the gate.
glossary: sweet bread rolls with small dried grapes in
a low glass box that keeps young plants warm
a garden tool with a long handle and metal teeth

texts.title: Where Do Shadows Come From?
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Original text. Facts from Royal Museums Greenwich, Human Sundial (KS2 resource), the national curriculum for Year 3 science and the NHS, Sunscreen and sun safety.
lines: On a sunny day, a dark shape follows you everywhere and copies every move you make. It is your shadow. But where does it come from?
What is a shadow?
Light comes from a light source, such as the Sun or a torch. Some materials, like wood and metal, block light. So does your body. Materials that block light are called opaque materials.
When an opaque object blocks the light, the light cannot reach the space behind it. That dark space is a shadow.
Which way do shadows point?
A shadow always points away from the light that makes it. If the Sun is in front of you, your shadow falls behind you.
Shadows on the move

The Sun seems to move across the sky during the day, so shadows move too. They move from west to east. In the morning, shadows are long. They get shorter towards the middle of the day, then grow longer again in the afternoon.
Stay safe in the Sun
Never look straight at the Sun, even if you are wearing sunglasses. It can damage your eyes for ever.
In the UK, the Sun is strongest between 11am and 3pm from March to October. Spend time in the shade then.
Try it

On a sunny day, stand on a chalk cross in the playground. Ask a partner to draw round your shadow in chalk and write the time next to it. Do it again at different times of the day. What happens to your shadow?
glossary: a place sheltered from the Sun’s light

texts.title: From a Railway Carriage
texts.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
texts.source: From A Child’s Garden of Verses by Robert Louis Stevenson, first published in 1885. Project Gutenberg eBook #136. Public domain in the UK.
lines: Faster than fairies, faster than witches,
Bridges and houses, hedges and ditches;
And charging along like troops in a battle
All through the meadows the horses and cattle:
All of the sights of the hill and the plain
Fly as thick as driving rain;
And ever again, in the wink of an eye,
Painted stations whistle by.
Here is a child who clambers and scrambles,
All by himself and gathering brambles;
Here is a tramp who stands and gazes;
And here is the green for stringing the daisies!
Here is a cart run away in the road
Lumping along with man and load;
And here is a mill, and there is a river:
Each a glimpse and gone forever!
glossary: long, narrow channels dug beside fields to carry water
a person with no home who walks from place to place
a grassy area in the middle of a village
moving along in a heavy, bumpy way

texts.title: How the Camel Got His Hump
texts.author: Rudyard Kipling
texts.source: From Just So Stories by Rudyard Kipling, first published in 1902: the opening of “How the Camel Got His Hump”. Project Gutenberg eBook #2781. Public domain in the UK.
lines: In the beginning of years, when the world was so new and all, and the
Animals were just beginning to work for Man, there was a Camel, and he
lived in the middle of a Howling Desert because he did not want to work; and
besides, he was a Howler himself. So he ate sticks and thorns and tamarisks
and milkweed and prickles, most ‘scruciating idle; and when anybody spoke to
him he said ‘Humph!’ Just ‘Humph!’ and no more.
Presently the Horse came to him on Monday morning, with a saddle on his
back and a bit in his mouth, and said, ‘Camel, O Camel, come out and trot like
the rest of us.’
‘Humph!’ said the Camel; and the Horse went away and told the Man.
Presently the Dog came to him, with a stick in his mouth, and said, ‘Camel,
O Camel, come and fetch and carry like the rest of us.’
‘Humph!’ said the Camel; and the Dog went away and told the Man.
Presently the Ox came to him, with the yoke on his neck and said, ‘Camel,
O Camel, come and plough like the rest of us.’
‘Humph!’ said the Camel; and the Ox went away and told the Man.
At the end of the day the Man called the Horse and the Dog and the Ox
together, and said, ‘Three, O Three, I’m very sorry for you (with the world so
new-and-all); but that Humph-thing in the Desert can’t work, or he would
have been here by now, so I am going to leave him alone, and you must work
double-time to make up for it.’
glossary: a wild, empty desert where the wind howls
bushy plants that grow in deserts
Kipling’s short way of saying excruciating, which here means terribly
a wooden bar fixed over an ox’s neck so it can pull a plough
to run at a steady pace, like a horse

texts.title: Mary Anning’s Great Find
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Original text. Facts from the Natural History Museum: Mary Anning: the unsung hero of fossil discovery and How are fossils formed? (nhm.ac.uk).
lines: Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a seaside town that is rich in fossils. Her father, Richard, made furniture and collected fossils too. He sold them from his shop.

In the autumn of 1811, when Mary was 12, her older brother Joseph found a strange-looking fossil skull. About a year later, in November 1812, Mary searched for the rest of the animal. She painstakingly dug out the outline of its skeleton. It was 5 metres long.
The creature was named Ichthyosaurus, which means “fish lizard”. We now know that it was neither a fish nor a lizard. It was a reptile that lived in the sea.

Mary kept searching. In December 1823, she became the first person to find a complete skeleton of a Plesiosaurus. In December 1828, she dug up a jumble of bones with a long tail and wings. It was a pterosaur, the first ever found outside Germany.

Mary’s finds were important, but the Geological Society of London would not let her join, because it did not allow women to become members. That did not change until long after her death. Mary died in 1847, when she was 47.
Timeline
1799: Mary is born
1811: Joseph finds the skull
1812: Mary digs out the skeleton
1823: Plesiosaurus
1828: pterosaur
1847: Mary dies
How does a fossil form?
1. An animal dies.
2. Its soft parts rot away.
3. It is buried under mud or sand.
4. Over a very long time, the layers build up and turn into rock.
5. Water seeps into the bones and teeth. It leaves minerals behind, which turn them to stone.
glossary: the remains of a plant or animal from long ago, preserved in rock
an animal with scaly skin, such as a lizard
a club for scientists who study rocks

texts.title: The Selfish Giant
texts.author: Oscar Wilde
texts.source: From “The Selfish Giant” in The Happy Prince and Other Tales by Oscar Wilde, first published in 1888: the opening of the story. Project Gutenberg eBook #902. Public domain in the UK.
lines: Every afternoon, as they were coming from school, the children used to go and
play in the Giant’s garden.
It was a large lovely garden, with soft green grass. Here and there over the
grass stood beautiful flowers like stars, and there were twelve peach-trees that
in the spring-time broke out into delicate blossoms of pink and pearl, and in the
autumn bore rich fruit. The birds sat on the trees and sang so sweetly that the
children used to stop their games in order to listen to them. “How happy we are
here!” they cried to each other.
One day the Giant came back. He had been to visit his friend the Cornish ogre,
and had stayed with him for seven years. After the seven years were over he
had said all that he had to say, for his conversation was limited, and he
determined to return to his own castle. When he arrived he saw the children
playing in the garden.
“What are you doing here?” he cried in a very gruff voice, and the children ran
away.
“My own garden is my own garden,” said the Giant; “any one can understand
that, and I will allow nobody to play in it but myself.” So he built a high wall all
round it, and put up a notice-board.
TRESPASSERS
WILL BE
PROSECUTED
He was a very selfish Giant.
The poor children had now nowhere to play. They tried to play on the road,
but the road was very dusty and full of hard stones, and they did not like it.
They used to wander round the high wall when their lessons were over, and talk
about the beautiful garden inside. “How happy we were there,” they said to each
other.
glossary: a cruel giant in fairy tales
people who go onto someone’s land without permission
taken to court to be punished

texts.title: A Letter from Stonehenge
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Original text. The facts about Stonehenge come from English Heritage, History of Stonehenge and Building Stonehenge (english-heritage.org.uk).
lines: 14th April
Dear Grandad,
Thank you for the fossil book you sent for my birthday. I have read half of it already!
Last Saturday, Mum and I visited Stonehenge. I had seen photos, but the stones were much bigger than I expected. We walked all the way round them on the path.
Our guide told us that people began building here about 5,000 years ago. The stone circle came later, in about 2500 BC. That is more than 4,000 years ago!

There are 2 kinds of stone. The big ones are called sarsens. They weigh about 25 tons each, and the biggest, the Heel Stone, weighs about 30 tons. They came from the Marlborough Downs, 20 miles away. The smaller stones are called bluestones. Each one weighs between 2 and 5 tons, and they came all the way from the Preseli Hills in Wales.

How did people move them without lorries or cranes? The builders had hammerstones, ropes made from plants, timber and picks made from antlers. The guide said they probably used a wooden frame to pull each stone upright.
My favourite fact is that 4 of the sarsens have carvings of axe-heads and daggers on them. They were carved hundreds of years after the circle was built.
I have bought you a postcard of the Heel Stone. I will bring it when we visit at half term.
Lots of love,
Amara
P.S. Please can we go together next time? You can be my guide!
glossary: used for dates long ago, counting back from the year 1
a unit for measuring very heavy things
the branching horns of a deer

texts.title: The Owl and the Pussy-Cat
texts.author: Edward Lear
texts.source: From Nonsense Songs by Edward Lear, first published in 1871 (text from Nonsense Books, Project Gutenberg eBook #13650). Public domain in the UK.
lines: The Owl and the Pussy-Cat went to sea
In a beautiful pea-green boat:
They took some honey, and plenty of money
Wrapped up in a five-pound note.
The Owl looked up to the stars above,
And sang to a small guitar,
“O lovely Pussy, O Pussy, my love,
What a beautiful Pussy you are,
You are,
You are!
What a beautiful Pussy you are!”
Pussy said to the Owl, “You elegant fowl,
How charmingly sweet you sing!
Oh! let us be married; too long we have tarried:
But what shall we do for a ring?”
They sailed away, for a year and a day,
To the land where the bong-tree grows;
And there in a wood a Piggy-wig stood,
With a ring at the end of his nose,
His nose,
His nose,
With a ring at the end of his nose.
“Dear Pig, are you willing to sell for one shilling
Your ring?” Said the Piggy, “I will.”
So they took it away, and were married next day
By the Turkey who lives on the hill.
They dined on mince and slices of quince,
Which they ate with a runcible spoon;
And hand in hand, on the edge of the sand,
They danced by the light of the moon,
The moon,
The moon,
They danced by the light of the moon.
glossary: an old coin: 20 shillings made 1 pound
a hard fruit rather like a pear

texts.title: The Railway Children
texts.author: E. Nesbit
texts.source: From The Railway Children by E. Nesbit, first published in 1906: part of Chapter 6. Project Gutenberg eBook #1874. Public domain in the UK.
lines: “Yes,” said Peter, slowly. He was still leaning on the fence. “Yes,” he said again,
still more slowly.
Then he stood upright.
“The 11.29 down hasn’t gone by yet. We must let them know at the station, or
there’ll be a most frightful accident.”
“Let’s run,” said Bobbie, and began.
But Peter cried, “Come back!” and looked at Mother’s watch. He was very
prompt and businesslike, and his face looked whiter than they had ever seen it.
“No time,” he said; “it’s two miles away, and it’s past eleven.”
“Couldn’t we,” suggested Phyllis, breathlessly, “couldn’t we climb up a
telegraph post and do something to the wires?”
“We don’t know how,” said Peter.
“They do it in war,” said Phyllis; “I know I’ve heard of it.”
“They only CUT them, silly,” said Peter, “and that doesn’t do any good. And we
couldn’t cut them even if we got up, and we couldn’t get up. If we had anything
red, we could get down on the line and wave it.”
“But the train wouldn’t see us till it got round the corner, and then it could
see the mound just as well as us,” said Phyllis; “better, because it’s much bigger
than us.”
“If we only had something red,” Peter repeated, “we could go round the corner
and wave to the train.”
“We might wave, anyway.”
“They’d only think it was just US, as usual. We’ve waved so often before.
Anyway, let’s get down.”
glossary: the train that is due at 11.29
a tall pole carrying wires that sent messages

texts.title: How the Egyptians Made a Mummy
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Original text. Facts from the Smithsonian Institution, Egyptian Mummies (si.edu), and the British Museum, Ancient Egypt (schools resources, britishmuseum.org).
lines: The ancient Egyptians believed that a person’s spirit needed a home after death, and that home was the body. If the body was destroyed, the spirit might be lost. So they preserved the body very carefully. A body preserved like this is called a mummy.
Making a mummy took 70 days. The people who did the work were called embalmers.
Step by step
1. The embalmers pushed long hooked tools up the nose and pulled out the brain, bit by bit.

2. They made a cut, usually on the left side of the body, and took out the organs inside. They left the heart in place, because they believed it was the most important part of a person, where their thinking came from.
3. Next, they covered the body with natron, a kind of salt that dries things out. They put packets of natron inside the body too.

4. When the body was completely dry, they took out the packets and gently washed off the natron. They filled any sunken parts with linen to make the body look more lifelike, and they added false eyes.

5. Priests wound long strips of linen around the body. At several stages, they coated the wrappings with warm resin. They tucked lucky charms called amulets in among the linen to protect the dead person.
Canopic jars

The stomach, liver, lungs and intestines were kept in special containers called canopic jars. The jars were decorated with the heads of the 4 sons of the god Horus: a human, a hawk, a baboon and a jackal.
glossary: parts inside the body that do a job, such as the stomach
a cloth made from the flax plant
a thick, sticky liquid that comes from some trees

texts.title: The North Wind and the Sun
texts.author: Inkworks Press, based on a fable by Aesop
texts.source: Original playscript by Inkworks Press, based on the plot of “The North Wind and the Sun” in Three Hundred Æsop’s Fables, translated by George Fyler Townsend (1867), Project Gutenberg eBook #21.
lines: Characters: NARRATOR, NORTH WIND, SUN, TRAVELLER
Setting: a country road on a cool day.
NARRATOR: High above a winding country road, the North Wind and the Sun were having an argument.
NORTH WIND: (puffing out his cheeks) I am the strongest thing in the sky. When I blow, trees bend and ships race across the sea.
SUN: (calmly) Being strong is not only about blowing hard, my friend.
NORTH WIND: Then let’s have a contest. Do you see that traveller on the road, in the long brown cloak?
SUN: I do.
NORTH WIND: Whoever can make him take off his cloak is the strongest. I’ll go first!
The North Wind blows. The Traveller stumbles and grips his cloak.
TRAVELLER: Brrr! Where did this wind come from? (He wraps the cloak tightly around himself.)
NORTH WIND: (blowing harder) Off! Off with it!
TRAVELLER: (bending into the wind) I’m not letting go of this cloak for anything!
NARRATOR: The harder the North Wind blew, the tighter the Traveller held on. At last, the North Wind gave up.
NORTH WIND: (out of breath) Go on, then. Let’s see what you can do.
The Sun smiles and shines warmly.
TRAVELLER: (looking up) Ah, that’s better. (He loosens his cloak.) It’s getting warm.
The Sun shines brighter still. The Traveller fans his face with his hat.
TRAVELLER: Phew! I’m far too hot for this heavy thing. (He takes off his cloak and folds it over his arm.) I’ll cool my feet in that stream.
The Traveller hurries off towards the stream.
SUN: (gently) You see? Gentle warmth can do what force cannot.
NARRATOR: And the North Wind had to agree.

texts.title: The River Bank
texts.author: Kenneth Grahame
texts.source: From The Wind in the Willows by Kenneth Grahame, first published in 1908: the opening of Chapter 1, “The River Bank”. Project Gutenberg eBook #289. Public domain in the UK.
lines: The Mole had been working very hard all the morning, spring-cleaning his little
home. First with brooms, then with dusters; then on ladders and steps and
chairs, with a brush and a pail of whitewash; till he had dust in his throat and
eyes, and splashes of whitewash all over his black fur, and an aching back and
weary arms. Spring was moving in the air above and in the earth below and
around him, penetrating even his dark and lowly little house with its spirit of
divine discontent and longing. It was small wonder, then, that he suddenly flung
down his brush on the floor, said “Bother!” and “O blow!” and also “Hang spring-
cleaning!” and bolted out of the house without even waiting to put on his coat.
Something up above was calling him imperiously, and he made for the steep
little tunnel which answered in his case to the gravelled carriage-drive owned by
animals whose residences are nearer to the sun and air. So he scraped and
scratched and scrabbled and scrooged and then he scrooged again and
scrabbled and scratched and scraped, working busily with his little paws and
muttering to himself, “Up we go! Up we go!” till at last, pop! his snout came out
into the sunlight, and he found himself rolling in the warm grass of a great
meadow.
“This is fine!” he said to himself. “This is better than whitewashing!” The
sunshine struck hot on his fur, soft breezes caressed his heated brow, and after
the seclusion of the cellarage he had lived in so long the carol of happy birds fell
on his dulled hearing almost like a shout. Jumping off all his four legs at once, in
the joy of living and the delight of spring without its cleaning, he pursued his
way across the meadow till he reached the hedge on the further side.
glossary: a white paint made from lime and water
a restless feeling of wanting something more
like an order that must be obeyed
being shut away on your own

texts.title: Hadrian’s Wall
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Original text. Facts from English Heritage, History of Hadrian’s Wall and Hadrian’s Wall: history and stories (english-heritage.org.uk).
lines: Hadrian’s Wall
A guide for young explorers
What is it?

Hadrian’s Wall is a wall that the Romans built across the north of England. It runs for 73 miles, from Wallsend on the River Tyne in the east to Bowness-on-Solway in the west. The Romans measured it as 80 Roman miles.
Who built it?

Hadrian was the Emperor of Rome from AD 117 to AD 138. He came to Britain in AD 122, and building probably began that year. The Wall was built by the 3 legions in Britain. Each legion had about 5,000 soldiers. The work took at least 6 years.
Did you know?
The newest Roman coins found on the Wall were made between AD 403 and AD 406.
Stone and turf
Most of the Wall was built of stone. The western 30 miles were built of turf: blocks of earth with grass on top.
Guarding the Wall

At every Roman mile there was a gate, protected by a small guard post called a milecastle. Between each pair of milecastles stood 2 towers called turrets. Before the work was finished, 14 forts were added too.
Life on the Wall
Soldiers from across Europe and North Africa served on the Wall. People from all these places met there and traded with each other.
glossary: the ruler of an empire: many lands ruled by a single person
used for dates counting forward from the year 1

units.title: Two Poems by Christina Rossetti
units.summary: In a poem, read each line as a small sentence. When a poem asks a question, look for where the answer comes.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 11 to 26. What does the poet say is red?
questions.explanation: Line 13 says “What is red? a poppy’s red”. A rose is the answer for pink.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 23 to 24. Find and copy the word that names what is violet.
questions.explanation: Line 23 says “clouds are violet”.

questions.prompt: “Sailing in the light” (line 18). What is the swan doing?
questions.explanation: Swans swim on water. Sailing here means gliding smoothly along, like a boat with a sail.
questions.misconception: Thinking the swan is in a real boat because of the word sailing.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 1 to 9. Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: Lines 3 and 7 say “Neither I nor you” and “Neither you nor I”. Nobody in the poem has seen the wind, but the leaves and trees show it is there.
questions.misconception: Reading the question “Who has seen the wind?” as if the poet is saying she saw it.

statements.s: The poet says she has seen the wind.
The leaves tremble when the wind passes.
The trees bow down their heads.
The poem says that you have seen the wind.

questions.prompt: Which thing goes with each colour in What is pink? Join them up.
questions.explanation: Each colour question is answered straight after it: lines 13, 21, 23 and 25.

questions.prompt: Put these colours in the order they come in What is pink?
questions.explanation: The poem goes pink, red, blue, white, yellow, then green, violet and orange. Each colour has 2 lines.

red
