questions.prompt: In Who has seen the wind?, how does the poet know the wind is there?
questions.explanation: The leaves hang trembling and the trees bow down their heads. We cannot see the wind, but we can see what it does.
options: She can see the wind’s colour.
She can see what it does to the leaves and the trees.

questions.prompt: Which pairs of words rhyme in What is pink? Choose all the right answers.
questions.explanation: Pink and brink end lines 11 and 12. White and light come in lines 17 and 18. Yellow and mellow come in lines 19 and 20. The other pairs do not sound alike at the end.

questions.prompt: How are the 2 poems alike?
questions.explanation: Line 2 asks “Who has seen the wind?” and line 11 asks “What is pink?”. Only the second poem is about colours.

questions.prompt: Ayesha thinks this poem shows that you can know something is there even when you cannot see it. Do you agree? Explain using Who has seen the wind?
questions.explanation: The poem is built on this idea: the wind is invisible, but its effects are not.
questions.model: Yes, I agree. The poet says nobody has seen the wind. But when “the leaves hang trembling” (line 4) and “the trees bow down their heads” (line 8), we know the wind is passing. We can see what it does, so we know it is there.
checklist: 1 mark: says that nobody can see the wind (Neither I nor you).
1 mark: uses the leaves or the trees as the clue that shows the wind is there.
Do not give the second mark for just copying a line with no explanation.

units.title: The Story of the Three Little Pigs
units.summary: Traditional tales often repeat words and events. Notice what stays the same and what changes, because the change is usually important.

questions.prompt: Look at line 12. What did the wolf do after he blew the straw house in?
questions.explanation: Line 12 says he “blew his house in, and ate up the little pig”.

questions.prompt: The third little pig met a man with a ___ of bricks.
questions.explanation: Line 21 says “a load of bricks”. The first 2 pigs met men with a bundle.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 5 to 6. Find and copy the word that tells you the wolf came along soon after the house was built.
questions.explanation: Presently is an old word for soon or a little later. Line 5 says “Presently came along a wolf”.
questions.misconception: Choosing knocked, which tells you what the wolf did, not when.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: The wolf says “Little pig, little pig, let me come in” 3 times, and each pig says no. Line 29 says he “could not get the house down”.
questions.misconception: Thinking the wolf blew down every house because he blew down the first 2.

statements.s: The wolf asks to come in at every house.
The pigs let the wolf in.
The man gave the third pig the bricks.
The wolf blew down the brick house.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen.
questions.explanation: The story follows each pig in turn, first, second, then third, and ends with the wolf failing at the brick house.
items: The old sow sends her pigs away.
The first pig asks a man for some straw.
The wolf eats the second pig.
The third pig builds a house of bricks.
The wolf cannot get the house down.

questions.prompt: Match each speaker to what they say.
questions.explanation: The wolf asks to come in, and the pig inside answers no. The first pig asks the man for straw in line 4.
pairs: “Little pig, little pig, let me come in.”
“No, no, by the hair of my chiny chin chin.”
the first pig, to the man
“Please, man, give me that straw to build me a house.”

questions.prompt: Why do you think the wolf could not blow the third house down?
questions.explanation: The wolf blew down houses of straw and furze, but not the house of bricks. The story does not say why, so you work it out: bricks are heavy and strong.
options: The third pig blew back at him.
Bricks are much stronger than straw or furze.
The wolf was too tired to blow.
The wind was blowing the other way.

questions.prompt: “No, no, by the hair of my chiny chin chin” (line 9). What does the pig mean?
questions.explanation: The pig is making a promise on his chin. Starting with “No, no” shows he is refusing to open the door.
questions.misconception: Taking the words literally and thinking the pig is talking about his hairy chin.
options: I will never let you in.

questions.prompt: How is what happens at the third house different from what happens at the first 2 houses? Use the story.
questions.explanation: Comparing means saying what is the same and what changes. Here the change is that the wolf fails.
questions.model: At the first 2 houses the wolf huffed and puffed and blew the house in, then ate the pig. At the brick house he “could not get the house down” (line 29), so the third pig stayed safe and the wolf had to try something else.
checklist: 1 mark: at the first 2 houses the wolf blew the house down and ate the pig.
1 mark: at the third house he could not blow it down, so the pig was safe.
Do not accept: the houses were made of different things, with nothing about what happened.

questions.prompt: Look at line 31. Do you think the third pig will be tricked by the wolf? Use what you know about the third pig from the story.
questions.explanation: A good prediction uses clues about a character from earlier in the story.
questions.model: No, I think the third pig will not be tricked. He was sensible enough to build his house of bricks, and the wolf “could not get the house down” (line 29). A pig that careful will probably guess the turnips are a trap.
checklist: 1 mark: a clear prediction (tricked or not tricked).
1 mark: a reason from the story about the third pig, for example he chose bricks, he did not let the wolf in, or the other pigs were eaten so he knows the wolf is dangerous.
Accept a prediction that he is tricked if it is backed by a reason from the text, for example he likes turnips or he has not been tricked before.

units.title: Grow a Bean in a Jar
units.summary: Instructions list what you need, then give the steps in order. Headings tell you which part to look at.

questions.prompt: What kind of seed do you need?
questions.explanation: Line 3, under You will need, says “1 broad bean seed”.

questions.prompt: Look at line 15. Find and copy the example the text gives of somewhere light.
questions.explanation: Step 5 says “such as a windowsill”. Such as is a signal that an example is coming.

questions.prompt: The paper should be “damp but not dripping” (line 12). What does damp mean?
questions.explanation: Damp means slightly wet. The text says not dripping, so it must not be soaking wet.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the right order.
questions.explanation: These are steps 1 to 5 under What to do. The numbers tell you the order.
items: Soak the bean in water.
Wet the folded kitchen paper.
Wrap the paper round the inside of the jar.
Push the bean between the paper and the glass.
Stand the jar somewhere light.

questions.prompt: Which things do you need? Choose all the right answers.
questions.explanation: Lines 3 to 6 list a bean, a jar, kitchen paper and a cup of water. Soil is mentioned in line 1, but only to say this method does not use it.
questions.misconception: Choosing soil because the word appears in the first line.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: Step 4 says push the bean in “about halfway up”. Line 9 says the shoot grows upwards. It is the root that grows downwards.

statements.s: You should check the paper every day.
If the paper feels dry, add a little water.
Push the bean right to the bottom of the jar.
The shoot grows downwards.

questions.prompt: Step 4 says to put the bean “where you can see it” (line 14). Why does this matter?
questions.explanation: The whole point of growing a bean in a jar is to watch it. Line 1 says that in soil everything happens out of sight.
options: so you can watch the root and shoot grow
so the bean gets less water
so the jar does not fall over

questions.prompt: Match each heading to what that part of the text tells you.
questions.explanation: Headings split instructions into parts, so you can find what you need quickly.
pairs: the things to collect before you start
the steps to follow in order
how the bean changes as it grows

questions.prompt: Leo’s paper dried out and his bean did not grow. Which step did Leo forget? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: This is a spot-the-mistake question. Find the step that would have stopped the problem.
questions.model: Leo forgot step 6: “Check the paper every day. If it feels dry, add a little water.” The bean needs water to grow, because the root “finds water and nutrients” (line 8). Dry paper gave it no water.
checklist: 1 mark: names step 6, or says he forgot to check the paper and add water.
1 mark: explains that the bean needs water to grow, using the text.
Do not accept: he forgot to soak the bean, with no link to the paper drying out.

questions.prompt: Imagine you keep your jar for another week. What do you think will happen to the shoot? Use the text.
questions.explanation: A prediction should come from what the text tells you, not a wild guess.
questions.model: I think the shoot will keep growing upwards and get taller, because the text says “The shoot grows upwards, towards the light” (line 9). It might grow more leaves too.
checklist: 1 mark: predicts the shoot will grow taller or keep growing.
1 mark: uses the text, for example that the shoot grows upwards towards the light.
Do not accept: a prediction about the root only.

units.title: The Tale of Peter Rabbit
units.summary: Writers tell you what characters are like through what they do. Look at the actions, then ask what they show.

questions.prompt: Where did Mrs. Rabbit go after she left her children?
questions.explanation: Lines 7 to 8 say she “went through the wood to the baker’s”.

questions.prompt: Look at line 8. Find and copy the kind of bread Mrs. Rabbit bought.
questions.explanation: Line 8 says “She bought a loaf of brown bread”.

questions.prompt: What did Peter eat in the garden? Choose all the right answers.
questions.explanation: Lines 13 to 14 say he ate lettuces, French beans and radishes. Flopsy, Mopsy and Cottontail gathered the blackberries, in the lane.
questions.misconception: Choosing blackberries, which the other rabbits picked, or carrots, which the text never mentions.

questions.prompt: Peter “squeezed under the gate” (line 12). Which words are closest in meaning to squeezed?
questions.explanation: To squeeze is to push into a space that is a tight fit. The gap under the gate was small.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: The other rabbits went down the lane. Line 21 says Peter “had forgotten the way back to the gate”.

statements.s: Mrs. Rabbit took her umbrella with her.
Flopsy, Mopsy and Cottontail went into the garden.
Mr. McGregor was planting young cabbages.
Peter remembered the way back to the gate.

questions.prompt: Match each character to what they did.
questions.explanation: Each character does something different. Only Peter goes into the garden.

questions.prompt: Start with the earliest. Put these in story order.
questions.explanation: The story moves forward in time. Peter only looks for parsley after eating so much that he feels sick (line 15).
items: Mrs. Rabbit warns her children about the garden.
Mrs. Rabbit sets off for the baker’s.
Peter eats some radishes.
Peter goes to look for some parsley.
Mr. McGregor chases Peter.

questions.prompt: Mr. McGregor ran after Peter “waving a rake” (line 19). What does this detail show?
questions.explanation: He is shouting “Stop thief!” and holding a garden tool with metal teeth. The detail makes the chase feel scary.
questions.misconception: Reading waving as a friendly wave.
options: Mr. McGregor is angry and Peter is in danger.
Mr. McGregor wants to play with Peter.
Mr. McGregor is tidying the garden.

questions.prompt: Maya thinks Mrs. Rabbit did not care where her children went. Is Maya right? Explain using lines 3 to 6.
questions.explanation: Mrs. Rabbit’s warning shows she is trying to protect them.
questions.model: No, Maya is wrong. Mrs. Rabbit tells her children where they may go, “into the fields or down the lane”, and warns them not to go into Mr. McGregor’s garden because their father was put in a pie there. She cares about keeping them safe.
checklist: 1 mark: says Maya is wrong.
1 mark: uses the warning about the garden or the danger to their father as evidence.
Do not give the second mark for just saying she is their mother.

questions.prompt: How is Peter different from Flopsy, Mopsy and Cottontail? Use the text.
questions.explanation: The writer puts the good bunnies and Peter next to each other so you notice the difference.
questions.model: Flopsy, Mopsy and Cottontail “were good little bunnies” (line 9). They did as they were told and gathered blackberries in the lane. Peter “was very naughty” (line 11) and ran straight to Mr. McGregor’s garden, the one place he was told not to go.
checklist: 1 mark: the other 3 were good, did as they were told, or went down the lane.
1 mark: Peter was naughty, disobeyed, or went into the garden.
Both sides must be described for 2 marks.

units.title: Where Do Shadows Come From?
units.summary: An information text gives facts. Use the headings to find the right section, then read that part carefully.

questions.prompt: Which of these does the text say blocks light?
questions.explanation: Line 3 says “Some materials, like wood and metal, block light.”

questions.prompt: Look at line 8. Find and copy the word that tells you what shadows are like in the morning.
questions.explanation: Line 8 says “In the morning, shadows are long.”

questions.prompt: “Light comes from a light source” (line 3). What is a light source?
questions.explanation: The text gives the Sun and a torch as examples. Both give out light.

questions.prompt: A shadow always points ___ from the light that makes it.
questions.explanation: Line 6 says “A shadow always points away from the light that makes it.”
questions.misconception: Writing towards, which is the opposite.

questions.prompt: Put these in order to show how your shadow changes during a sunny day.
questions.explanation: Line 8 describes the whole day in order: long, shorter, then longer again.
items: Your shadow is long in the morning.
It gets shorter towards the middle of the day.
It grows longer again in the afternoon.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: A shadow is a dark space (line 4). Line 11 says the Sun is strongest from March to October.

statements.s: Wood and metal block light.
A shadow is a bright space.
If the Sun is in front of you, your shadow falls behind you.
In the UK, the Sun is strongest from November to February.

questions.prompt: Your shadow “copies every move you make” (line 1). What does this mean?
questions.explanation: To copy is to do the same thing. When you wave, your shadow waves too.
options: It makes a noise when you move.

questions.prompt: Match each heading to what that section tells you.
questions.explanation: Each heading is a clue to what its section is about.
pairs: how shadows change during the day
how to keep safe in strong sunshine

questions.prompt: Priya thinks she will still have a shadow if she stands in a dark room with no light at all. Is Priya right? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Use what the text says a shadow is, then apply it to a new situation.
questions.model: No, Priya is wrong. A shadow is made when an opaque object blocks the light, so the light “cannot reach the space behind it” (line 4). If there is no light at all, there is nothing to block, so there is no shadow.
checklist: 1 mark: says Priya is wrong.
1 mark: explains that a shadow needs light to be blocked, using the text.
Do not give the second mark for it is too dark to see with no reason about light being blocked.

questions.prompt: In the Try it activity, you draw round your shadow in the morning and again in the middle of the day. What do you think you will notice? Use the text.
questions.explanation: Predicting from facts means using what the text has told you.
questions.model: I think the middle-of-the-day shadow will be shorter than the morning one, because shadows “get shorter towards the middle of the day” (line 8). It will also be in a different place, because shadows move as the Sun seems to move across the sky.
checklist: 1 mark: predicts the shadow will be shorter (or will have moved).
1 mark: backs this up with a fact from the text.
Accept: the shadow will point a different way.

units.title: From a Railway Carriage
units.summary: A poem can make you feel speed or calm through its words and rhythm. Picture each thing the poet describes.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 9 to 10. What is the child gathering?
questions.explanation: Line 10 says “gathering brambles”. The word box says brambles here means blackberries.

questions.prompt: Look at line 15. Find and copy the word that names a building.
questions.explanation: Line 15 says “here is a mill, and there is a river”. A river is not a building.

questions.prompt: “Fly as thick as driving rain” (line 6). What is driving rain?
questions.explanation: Driving rain is heavy rain pushed along by the wind. The sights rush past like it.
questions.misconception: Thinking driving means driving a car.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: Line 11 says the tramp “stands and gazes”. The cart has “run away” and is “Lumping along” (lines 13 to 14), so it is not careful.

statements.s: The horses and cattle are in the meadows.
The tramp is running.
The cart is moving slowly and carefully.
There is a river.

questions.prompt: Put these sights in the order they come in the poem.
questions.explanation: The poem lists the sights one after another as the train passes them.
items: bridges and houses
horses and cattle
painted stations
a child gathering brambles
a mill and a river

questions.prompt: Look at line 7. Find and copy the words that tell you how quickly the stations go by.
questions.explanation: A wink takes less than a second, so in the wink of an eye means almost instantly.
questions.answer: in the wink of an eye

questions.prompt: The poem is written in rhyming pairs of lines. Match each word to the word it rhymes with.
questions.explanation: Each pair ends 2 lines next to each other: lines 5 and 6, 9 and 10, 11 and 12, 13 and 14.

questions.prompt: Which of these words from the poem make you think of speed? Choose all the right answers.
questions.explanation: Charging means rushing forward, whistle by means zooming past, and a glimpse is a very quick look. Stands and gazes describe the tramp keeping still.
questions.misconception: Choosing any verb, even ones that describe keeping still.

questions.prompt: Why do so many lines start with “Here is” (lines 9 to 15)?
questions.explanation: Each “Here is” is like pointing out of the window as something new appears, then it is gone.
options: to show the train has stopped
to tell you where the train is going
to show each new thing suddenly coming into view

questions.prompt: Who is telling this poem, and where are they? Explain how you know.
questions.explanation: Inference means working something out from clues. The poem never says I am on a train.
questions.model: The person telling the poem is riding on a train and looking out of the window. Everything goes past very fast: “Painted stations whistle by” (line 8) and each sight is “a glimpse and gone forever” (line 16). Only someone moving quickly would see things flash past like that.
checklist: 1 mark: says the speaker is on a train (or in a railway carriage) looking out.
1 mark: gives a clue from the poem, such as things whistling by, or seeing each thing only for a glimpse.
Accept the title as one clue if a line from the poem is also used.

units.title: How the Camel Got His Hump
units.summary: Some stories repeat a pattern. Spot what happens each time, then think about why the writer repeats it.

questions.prompt: On which day did the Horse come to see the Camel?
questions.explanation: Line 7 says “the Horse came to him on Monday morning”.

questions.prompt: Look at line 6. Find and copy the word the Camel said when anybody spoke to him.
questions.explanation: Line 6 says “he said ‘Humph!’ Just ‘Humph!’ and no more.”

questions.prompt: What did the Camel eat? Choose all the right answers.
questions.explanation: Lines 4 to 5 say he ate “sticks and thorns and tamarisks and milkweed and prickles”. Grass and carrots are not in the list.

questions.prompt: “Presently the Dog came to him” (line 11). What does presently mean here?
questions.explanation: Presently is an old word for soon or after a while. It has nothing to do with presents.
questions.misconception: Linking presently to the word present (a gift).

questions.prompt: Match each animal to what it had with it.
questions.explanation: Lines 7, 11 and 14 tell you what each animal had. Each one shows the work that animal does.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: Line 3 says the Camel “did not want to work”. Line 19 shows the Man thinks the Camel “can’t work”.
questions.misconception: Missing the word can’t and reading the Man’s words the wrong way round.

statements.s: The Camel lived in a desert.
The Camel wanted to work.
The Man called the animals together at the end of the day.
The Man said the Camel was able to work.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen.
questions.explanation: The animals come one by one: the Horse, then the Dog, then the Ox. The Man speaks at the end of the day.
items: The Horse asks the Camel to trot.
The Dog asks the Camel to fetch and carry.
The Ox asks the Camel to plough.
The Man calls the animals together.
The Man decides to leave the Camel alone.

questions.prompt: The Man says the Camel “can’t work” (line 19). Why does the Man think this?
questions.explanation: The Man says the Camel “would have been here by now” if he could work. He does not know the Camel simply will not.
options: The Camel told the Man he was ill.
The Camel never came, so the Man thought he was not able to.
The Horse said the Camel was too small.

questions.prompt: The Camel answers everybody with just 1 word. What does this show about him?
questions.explanation: Each animal asks politely, and the Camel just says Humph and carries on doing nothing. That is rude and lazy.
options: He cannot speak any other words.
He is rude and cannot be bothered.

questions.prompt: How is the Camel different from the Horse, the Dog and the Ox? Use the text.
questions.explanation: Comparing means describing both sides, not just one.
questions.model: The Horse, the Dog and the Ox all work for Man. They trot, fetch and carry, and plough, and they come to ask the Camel to join them. The Camel “did not want to work” (line 3). He stays in the desert and just says Humph.
checklist: 1 mark: the other animals work (or do jobs for Man, or are willing to help).
1 mark: the Camel refuses to work, is idle, or only says Humph.
Both sides must be described for 2 marks.

units.title: Mary Anning’s Great Find
units.summary: A recount tells real events in time order. Dates and time words such as later help you follow what happened when.

questions.prompt: Mary grew up by the sea. Which town was she born in?
questions.explanation: Line 1 says she was born “in Lyme Regis, a seaside town that is rich in fossils”.

questions.prompt: Look at line 1. Find and copy the word that tells you what Mary’s father made.
questions.explanation: Line 1 says her father “made furniture and collected fossils too”.

questions.prompt: Which of these did Mary find? Choose all the right answers.
questions.explanation: Mary dug out the Ichthyosaurus skeleton in 1812, found the Plesiosaurus in 1823 and the pterosaur in 1828. Her brother Joseph found the skull.
questions.misconception: Thinking Mary found the skull, when the text says Joseph did.

questions.prompt: “a jumble of bones” (line 4). What does jumble mean?
questions.explanation: A jumble is a mess of things mixed together. The bones were not laid out neatly.

questions.prompt: Match each year to what happened.
questions.explanation: All these years are in the text and on the timeline (lines 7 to 12).

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: Line 3 says it was “neither a fish nor a lizard”. It was a reptile that lived in the sea. Line 5 says the Society would not let her join.
questions.misconception: Believing the name, fish lizard, tells you what the animal really was.

statements.s: Ichthyosaurus means “fish lizard”.
An Ichthyosaurus was a kind of fish.
The pterosaur had wings.
The Geological Society let Mary join.

questions.prompt: Look at How does a fossil form? Put these steps in order.
questions.explanation: Lines 14 to 18 number the steps 1 to 5.
items: An animal dies.
Its soft parts rot away.
It is buried under mud or sand.
The layers turn into rock.
Minerals turn the bones and teeth to stone.

questions.prompt: How many years were there between Mary finding the Plesiosaurus and finding the pterosaur?
questions.explanation: The Plesiosaurus was in 1823 and the pterosaur in 1828. 1828 take away 1823 is 5.

questions.prompt: Why does the text have a timeline as well as the main writing?
questions.explanation: The timeline repeats the key dates from the writing in a short list, so they are quick to find.
options: to tell you new facts that are not in the writing
so you can see the main dates in order at a glance
to show what Mary looked like

questions.prompt: The text says Mary’s finds were important. Find 2 pieces of evidence in the text that show this.
questions.explanation: Evidence means facts from the text that back up a statement.
questions.model: She was “the first person to find a complete skeleton of a Plesiosaurus” (line 4). Her pterosaur was “the first ever found outside Germany” (line 4). Being the first to find something shows it was important.
checklist: 1 mark for each piece of evidence, up to 2: first complete Plesiosaurus; first pterosaur found outside Germany; the Ichthyosaurus skeleton was 5 metres long and was given a name.
Do not accept: she was born in Lyme Regis, or a fact that does not show importance.

units.title: The Selfish Giant
units.summary: Writers show how characters feel through what they say and do. Compare the start of a story with what comes later.

questions.prompt: How many peach-trees were in the garden?
questions.explanation: Line 4 says “there were twelve peach-trees”. The Giant was away for 7 years, which is a different number.

questions.prompt: Look at line 9. Find and copy the word that tells you what kind of creature the Giant’s friend was.
questions.explanation: Line 9 says he had been “to visit his friend the Cornish ogre”.

questions.prompt: “delicate blossoms of pink and pearl” (line 5). What does delicate mean?
questions.explanation: Delicate things are fine and fragile. Blossom petals are soft and fall easily.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: The Giant cried “What are you doing here?” and the children ran away. Line 24 says “they did not like it” on the road.
questions.misconception: Thinking the children were happy anywhere, without checking line 24.

statements.s: The Giant had been to visit the Cornish ogre.
The Giant asked the children to stay.
The road was dusty and full of hard stones.
The children liked playing on the road.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen.
questions.explanation: The extract moves through time: happy play, the Giant returns, the wall goes up, and the children are left outside.
items: The children play in the Giant’s garden.
The Giant comes back from the Cornish ogre.
The children run away.
The Giant builds a high wall.
The children wander round the wall.

questions.prompt: Match each speaker to their words.
questions.explanation: Speech marks show the exact words. Check who is speaking just before or after each one.
pairs: “My own garden is my own garden,”

questions.prompt: “the children used to stop their games in order to listen to them” (lines 6 to 7). What does this tell you about the birds’ singing?
questions.explanation: Line 6 says the birds “sang so sweetly”. Stopping a game to listen shows how beautiful it was.
options: It was a warning that the Giant was coming.
It made the children want to go home.
It was so lovely that the children wanted to hear it.
It was so loud that the children could not play.

questions.prompt: “his conversation was limited” (line 11). What does this tell you about the Giant?
questions.explanation: Limited means there was not much of it. After 7 years he had run out of things to say, so he went home.
questions.misconception: Thinking limited means the Giant was not allowed to speak.
options: He could only speak in a whisper.
He did not like his friend.
He did not have much to talk about.

questions.prompt: How do the children feel at the end of the extract? Explain how you know.
questions.explanation: Feelings are often shown, not told. Look at what the children do and say.
questions.model: The children feel sad and miss the garden. The writer calls them “The poor children” (line 23) because they have nowhere to play. They wander round the wall and say “How happy we were there,” (line 26), which shows they are not happy now.
checklist: 1 mark: a feeling such as sad, upset, unhappy or missing the garden.
1 mark: evidence such as the poor children, nowhere to play, wandering round the wall, or How happy we were there.
Do not accept: happy, unless it refers only to the past.

questions.prompt: Compare the garden with the road where the children try to play. Use the text.
questions.explanation: The writer makes the road sound unpleasant so you understand what the children have lost.
questions.model: The garden had “soft green grass” (line 3), flowers like stars, peach-trees and birds that sang sweetly. The road was “very dusty and full of hard stones” (line 24). The garden was soft and beautiful, but the road was hard and dirty.
checklist: 1 mark: a detail about the garden (soft green grass, flowers, peach-trees, birds).
1 mark: a detail about the road (dusty, hard stones), making the difference clear.
Both places must be described for 2 marks.

units.title: A Letter from Stonehenge
units.summary: A letter starts with a date and a greeting and ends with a sign-off. Read it to find out facts and how the writer feels.

questions.prompt: Who did Amara visit Stonehenge with?
questions.explanation: Line 4 says “Mum and I visited Stonehenge.” Grandad was not there, which is why Amara writes to him.

questions.prompt: Look at line 6. Find and copy the name of the biggest stone.
questions.explanation: Line 6 says “the biggest, the Heel Stone, weighs about 30 tons”.

questions.prompt: “They were carved hundreds of years after the circle was built” (line 8). What does carved mean?
questions.explanation: Carving means cutting shapes into something hard. The axe-heads and daggers were cut into the stone.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: Line 4 says the stones “were much bigger than I expected”. Line 9 says she will bring the postcard when they visit.
questions.misconception: Mixing up bigger and smaller when reading quickly.

statements.s: Amara walked round the stones on the path.
The stones were smaller than Amara expected.
The stone circle was built in about 2500 BC.
Amara has already given Grandad the postcard.

questions.prompt: Which of these did the builders have? Choose all the right answers.
questions.explanation: Line 7 lists hammerstones, ropes made from plants, timber and picks made from antlers. It asks how they managed without lorries or cranes.
questions.misconception: Choosing cranes or lorries because they are named in the same line.

questions.prompt: Put these parts of the letter in the order they come.
questions.explanation: A letter has a set shape: date, greeting, the main part, a sign-off, and sometimes a P.S. added at the very end.
items: the date
Dear Grandad,
thank you for the fossil book
facts about the stones
Lots of love,
the P.S.

questions.prompt: How many miles did the sarsens travel to reach Stonehenge?
questions.explanation: Line 6 says the sarsens “came from the Marlborough Downs, 20 miles away”.

questions.prompt: Match each number to what it tells you.
questions.explanation: Each number comes from a different part of the letter (lines 5, 6 and 8). Read the words around a number to see what it describes.
pairs: the weight of each big sarsen
the weight of the Heel Stone
how long ago people began building here

questions.prompt: Why does Amara write “That is more than 4,000 years ago!” (line 5)?
questions.explanation: The exclamation mark shows surprise. Amara is impressed that the circle is so very old.
options: She is bored of the facts.
She is amazed at how old the stone circle is.

questions.prompt: Find 2 things in the letter that show Amara listened carefully to the guide.
questions.explanation: The letter says Our guide told us and The guide said. Those phrases point to the evidence.
questions.model: Amara remembers that people “began building here about 5,000 years ago” (line 5), which the guide told them. She also remembers that the guide said they “probably used a wooden frame to pull each stone upright” (line 7).
checklist: 1 mark for each fact that the letter says came from the guide, up to 2: building began about 5,000 years ago; the circle came later in about 2500 BC; they probably used a wooden frame.
Also accept: she can name the 2 kinds of stone and where they came from, if the child links it to what she learned on the visit.

units.title: The Owl and the Pussy-Cat
units.summary: A narrative poem tells a story. Nonsense poems are meant to be fun and can use made-up words.

questions.prompt: What did the Owl sing to?
questions.explanation: Line 6 says he “sang to a small guitar”.

questions.prompt: Look at line 26. Find and copy the name of the animal who married them.
questions.explanation: Line 26 says they were married “By the Turkey who lives on the hill”.

questions.prompt: Pussy calls the Owl an “elegant fowl” (line 12). Which of these is closest to what she means?
questions.explanation: Elegant means graceful and stylish. The word box says fowl means a bird. The Pussy-Cat is paying the Owl a compliment.
options: You are a graceful, smart-looking bird.
You are a very old bird.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: The ring was “at the end of his nose” (line 19). They were married by the Turkey “who lives on the hill” (line 26), not at sea.
questions.misconception: Guessing that the wedding happened on the boat because they went to sea.

statements.s: They sailed away for a year and a day.
The Piggy-wig had a ring on his tail.
They ate with a runcible spoon.
They were married on the boat.

questions.prompt: Put these parts of the story in the order the poem tells them.
questions.explanation: The poem tells the story in time order, from setting off to the wedding feast.
items: They pack some honey and money.
The Owl sings to the Pussy-Cat.
The Pussy-Cat asks what they will do for a ring.
They buy the ring from the Piggy-wig.
They dine on mince and slices of quince.

questions.prompt: Match each question to its answer from the poem.
questions.explanation: The answers are in lines 18, 25, 27 and 29.
pairs: on the edge of the sand

questions.prompt: Some lines have 2 rhyming words inside them. Which of these pairs rhyme inside a line? Choose all the right answers.
questions.explanation: Honey and money are in line 3, married and tarried in line 14, and mince and quince in line 27. These rhymes make the poem bouncy and fun to read aloud.

questions.prompt: Lines 9 and 10 repeat “You are” (lines 9 to 10). Why do you think the poet does this?
questions.explanation: The Owl is singing, and songs often repeat words. Saying it again and again shows how strongly he feels.
options: to make it sound like a song and show how much the Owl means it
because the Owl has forgotten the words
to tell you the Pussy-Cat is sad

questions.prompt: Why did the Owl and the Pussy-Cat buy the Pig’s ring?
questions.explanation: In line 15 the Pussy-Cat asks “But what shall we do for a ring?” Then they find the Pig with a ring and are married the next day.
options: They wanted to give it to the Turkey.
The Pig was selling it cheaply.
They needed a ring to get married.
They wanted to pay for their dinner.

questions.prompt: Find 2 clues that show this is a nonsense poem and not a true story.
questions.explanation: Nonsense poems are meant to be silly. Look for things that could not happen and words that are not real.
questions.model: An owl and a cat could not really sail to sea and get married, and a turkey could not marry them. The poem also uses made-up words, such as “runcible spoon” (line 28) and “bong-tree” (line 17).
checklist: 1 mark for each clue, up to 2: animals talking, singing or marrying; an owl and a cat in a boat; a pig selling a ring; a turkey holding a wedding; made-up words such as runcible or bong-tree.
Do not accept: it rhymes (true poems rhyme too).

units.title: The Railway Children
units.summary: Dialogue shows what characters think and feel. Look at what they say and how they say it.

questions.prompt: What was Peter leaning on at the start?
questions.explanation: Line 1 says “He was still leaning on the fence.”

questions.prompt: Look at line 7. Find and copy whose watch Peter looked at.
questions.explanation: Line 7 says he “looked at Mother’s watch”.

questions.prompt: “a most frightful accident” (line 5). What does frightful mean?
questions.explanation: Frightful comes from fright. A frightful accident would be very bad and scary.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: The children keep wishing they had “something red”, so nobody has a flag. Phyllis says the train “wouldn’t see us till it got round the corner” (line 17).
questions.misconception: Assuming the children have a flag because waving something red is their plan.

statements.s: Bobbie wants to run to the station.
Phyllis has a red flag.
Peter says they couldn’t cut the wires even if they got up.
The train will be able to see the children from far away.

questions.prompt: Match each child to what they say.
questions.explanation: Look for the name after each piece of speech: “said Bobbie” (line 6), “said Phyllis” (line 13) and “said Peter” (line 12).

questions.prompt: Why does Phyllis think waving on the line might not help?
questions.explanation: Lines 17 to 19 explain that by then the train could see the mound itself, and the mound is much bigger than the children.
options: It was too dark to see.
The train would not see them until it got round the corner.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen.
questions.explanation: The children’s ideas come one after another, as they argue about what to do.
items: Peter says the 11.29 has not gone by yet.
Bobbie starts to run.
Peter calls her back.
Phyllis suggests climbing a telegraph post.
Peter says they need something red.

questions.prompt: “They only CUT them, silly,” (line 14). Why is CUT written in capital letters?
questions.explanation: Capital letters in the middle of speech show which word is said with extra force. Peter is correcting Phyllis firmly.
options: to show Peter says it strongly

questions.prompt: “Let’s run,” (line 6) said Bobbie, and began. What does this show about Bobbie?
questions.explanation: Bobbie does not wait. As soon as she hears of the danger, she starts running to warn the station.
options: She is scared and wants to go home.
She acts quickly to try to help.
She does not care about the train.
She wants to race Peter for fun.

questions.prompt: What does this extract tell you about the children? Use the text to explain.
questions.explanation: Describe what the children are like, then prove it with something they say or do.
questions.model: The children are brave and caring, because they want to stop “a most frightful accident” (line 5) even though nobody asked them to. They think quickly too: Bobbie starts to run, Phyllis suggests the telegraph post and Peter thinks of waving something red.
checklist: 1 mark: a sensible point about the children, such as brave, caring, quick-thinking, sensible or worried.
1 mark: evidence from the text that supports the point.
Do not accept: a retelling of what happens with no point about what the children are like.

units.title: How the Egyptians Made a Mummy
units.summary: A process is a set of steps done in a fixed order. Numbered steps and time words such as next help you follow it.

questions.prompt: What were the people who made mummies called?
questions.explanation: Line 2 says “The people who did the work were called embalmers.” Priests did the wrapping in step 5.

questions.prompt: Look at line 6. Find and copy the name of the salt that dries things out.
questions.explanation: Line 6 says “natron, a kind of salt that dries things out”.

questions.prompt: “They filled any sunken parts with linen” (line 7). What does sunken mean?
questions.explanation: When a body dries out, some parts sink inwards. Filling them with linen made the body look more lifelike.

questions.prompt: Which organs were kept in canopic jars? Choose all the right answers.
questions.explanation: Line 10 lists the stomach, liver, lungs and intestines. The heart was left in place, and the brain was pulled out in step 1.
questions.misconception: Choosing the heart, which was left inside the body.

questions.prompt: Match each thing to what it was used for.
questions.explanation: Steps 3 to 5 (lines 6 to 8) explain what each thing was for.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: Line 5 says the cut was “usually on the left side”. It also says they believed the heart was “where their thinking came from”.
questions.misconception: Using what we know today (thinking happens in the brain) instead of what the Egyptians believed.

statements.s: The cut was usually made on the right side of the body.
The embalmers added false eyes.
Priests wound strips of linen around the body.
The Egyptians believed thinking came from the brain.

questions.prompt: Put these jobs in the order the embalmers did them.
questions.explanation: Follow the numbered steps 1 to 5 (lines 4 to 8).
items: pulled out the brain
took out the organs
covered the body with natron
added false eyes
coated the wrappings with resin

questions.prompt: Why do you think the embalmers added false eyes?
questions.explanation: Step 4 is all about making the body look “more lifelike”, so false eyes fit that job.
options: to help the brain dry out
to make the body look more like a living person

questions.prompt: “At several stages, they coated the wrappings with warm resin” (line 8). What does at several stages tell you?
questions.explanation: Several means more than 2, and a stage is one part of a process. So the resin was added a number of times during the wrapping.
questions.misconception: Thinking stage means a stage in a theatre.
options: They did it more than once, at different times.
They did it on a stage in front of people.
They did it only at the very end.

questions.prompt: Explain why the steps had to be done in this order. Use 2 steps in your answer.
questions.explanation: In a process, each step often depends on the one before it.
questions.model: The body had to be dried with natron before it was wrapped, because the embalmers waited until “the body was completely dry” (line 7) before washing off the natron. Only then could the priests wind the linen around it in step 5. Wrapping a wet body would not have worked.
checklist: 1 mark: names 2 steps in the right order.
1 mark: explains why one has to come before the other, using the text (for example the body must be dry before it is wrapped).
Do not accept: the steps are numbered, with no reason.

units.title: The North Wind and the Sun
units.summary: A playscript shows who speaks with their name. Words in brackets are stage directions that tell actors what to do.

questions.prompt: What colour is the Traveller’s cloak?
questions.explanation: Line 6 says “the long brown cloak”.

questions.prompt: Look at line 18. Find and copy where the Traveller wants to cool his feet.
questions.explanation: Line 18 says “I’ll cool my feet in that stream.”

questions.prompt: “The Traveller stumbles and grips his cloak” (line 9). What does stumbles mean?
questions.explanation: The strong wind pushes the Traveller so he loses his balance for a moment.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: The North Wind says “I’ll go first!” (line 8). In the end the Traveller takes off his cloak for the Sun, so the Sun wins.
questions.misconception: Thinking the North Wind wins because he is so loud and strong.

statements.s: The play is set on a cool day.
The Sun has the first turn in the contest.
The Traveller fans his face with his hat.
The North Wind wins the contest.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen.
questions.explanation: The play follows the contest from the argument to the ending.
items: The North Wind boasts that he is the strongest.
They agree to have a contest.
The North Wind gives up.
The Sun shines warmly.
The Traveller takes off his cloak.

questions.prompt: Match each stage direction to the character it is for.
questions.explanation: A stage direction comes straight after the name of the character who does it (lines 11, 12 and 20).

questions.prompt: Why does the Traveller loosen his cloak in line 16?
questions.explanation: The Sun has just started shining warmly, and the Traveller says “It’s getting warm.”
options: It is too small for him.
He is starting to feel warm.
He wants to give it away.
The wind has blown it open.

questions.prompt: How is the Sun different from the North Wind?
questions.explanation: The Sun speaks “(calmly)” and “(gently)”. The North Wind boasts and blows harder and harder.
options: The Sun is louder than the North Wind.
The Sun wants to win, but the North Wind does not.
The Sun is calm and gentle, but the North Wind boasts and uses force.
The Sun gives up, but the North Wind keeps going.

questions.prompt: “Gentle warmth can do what force cannot” (line 20). What does force mean here?
questions.explanation: Force here means strength used roughly, like the North Wind blowing as hard as he can.

questions.prompt: The North Wind says, “I am the strongest thing in the sky.” (line 4) Has he been proved right by the end of the play? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Check a character’s claim against what actually happens in the story.
questions.model: No. He set the test himself: whoever makes the Traveller take off his cloak “is the strongest”. The harder he blew, the tighter the Traveller held on, and he “gave up” (line 13). The Sun’s warmth made the Traveller take off his cloak, and the North Wind “had to agree” (line 21).
checklist: 1 mark: says he has not been proved right (the Sun wins).
1 mark: evidence from the play, such as the Traveller holding on tighter, the North Wind giving up, or the Traveller taking off his cloak for the Sun.
Do not accept: yes, because he blows very hard.

units.title: The River Bank
units.summary: Writers choose words carefully to help you picture a scene and share a character’s feelings. Think about why a word was chosen.

questions.prompt: What was Mole doing all morning?
questions.explanation: Line 1 says he “had been working very hard all the morning, spring-cleaning his little home”.

questions.prompt: Look at line 9. Find and copy what Mole did not wait to put on.
questions.explanation: Line 9 says he left “without even waiting to put on his coat”.

questions.prompt: “soft breezes caressed his heated brow” (line 19). What does caressed mean?
questions.explanation: To caress is to stroke softly. The breeze feels kind and cool on Mole’s hot head.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: Line 4 mentions “his black fur”. Line 23 says he walked on “till he reached the hedge”.
questions.misconception: Guessing a mole’s colour instead of checking the text.

statements.s: Mole had whitewash on his fur.
Mole had brown fur.
Mole used a tunnel to get outside.
Mole stopped when he reached a river.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 1 to 3. Put these in the order the text mentions them.
questions.explanation: Line 2 says “First with brooms, then with dusters”. The words first and then show the order.
items: brooms
dusters
ladders and steps and chairs
a brush and a pail of whitewash

questions.prompt: What did Mole say when he flung down his brush? Choose all the right answers.
questions.explanation: Line 8 says he said “Bother!” and “O blow!” (and also Hang spring-cleaning!). He said Up we go! later in the tunnel, and This is fine! in the meadow.
questions.misconception: Choosing words Mole says later, without checking when he says them.

questions.prompt: Match each word from the text to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Use the sentence around each word: weary arms (line 5), flung down his brush (lines 7 to 8), muttering to himself (line 15), pursued his way across the meadow (lines 22 to 23).

questions.prompt: “pop! his snout came out into the sunlight” (lines 15 to 16). Why does the writer use the word pop?
questions.explanation: Pop is a short, sudden sound. After all the digging, Mole’s nose suddenly breaks through into the light.
options: It tells you Mole hurt his nose.
It sounds sudden, as if Mole bursts out all at once.
It is the noise of a bird singing.

questions.prompt: “the carol of happy birds fell on his dulled hearing almost like a shout” (lines 20 to 21). What does this tell you?
questions.explanation: Mole had lived in the quiet cellarage “so long”. Even happy birdsong sounded loud to him.
questions.misconception: Taking almost like a shout literally, as if the birds really shouted.
options: Mole could not hear the birds.
The birds were angry with Mole.
After being underground so long, the birdsong seemed very loud to Mole.
The birds were shouting at Mole.

questions.prompt: How does Mole feel when he reaches the meadow? Give 2 pieces of evidence from the text.
questions.explanation: Use Mole’s words and actions as evidence for his feelings.
questions.model: Mole feels happy and free. He says “This is fine!” and “This is better than whitewashing!” (line 18). He jumps “off all his four legs at once” in “the joy of living” (lines 21 to 22).
checklist: 1 mark: a feeling such as happy, excited, joyful or free.
1 mark: 2 pieces of evidence, for example This is fine!, better than whitewashing, jumping off all 4 legs, the joy of living, the delight of spring.
Give 1 mark only if the feeling is right but just 1 piece of evidence is given.

units.title: Hadrian’s Wall
units.summary: A leaflet gives information in short sections with headings, so readers can find facts quickly.

questions.prompt: Which river is Wallsend on?
questions.explanation: Line 4 says “from Wallsend on the River Tyne in the east”.

questions.prompt: Look at line 12. Find and copy the name for the towers between the milecastles.
questions.explanation: Line 12 says “stood 2 towers called turrets”.

questions.prompt: How many Roman miles long did the Romans measure the Wall to be?
questions.explanation: Line 4 says “The Romans measured it as 80 Roman miles.” The 73 miles is the length in our miles.
questions.misconception: Giving 73, which is the length in our miles.

questions.prompt: “building probably began that year” (line 6). What does probably tell you?
questions.explanation: Probably means very likely. Historians do not have a record that says exactly when building began.
options: The writer thinks this is likely but is not completely sure.

questions.prompt: Is each sentence true or false?
questions.explanation: Line 6 says Hadrian came to Britain in AD 122 and building probably began that year. Line 14 says soldiers came “from across Europe and North Africa”.
questions.misconception: Mixing up the different AD dates in the same section.

statements.s: Hadrian was Emperor from AD 117 to AD 138.
Building probably began in AD 138.
The Wall runs across the north of England.
All the soldiers on the Wall came from Britain.

questions.prompt: Use the dates to put these events in order.
questions.explanation: AD 117, AD 122, AD 138, then AD 403 to AD 406. With AD dates, a bigger number is later.
items: Hadrian becomes Emperor.
Hadrian comes to Britain and building probably begins.
Hadrian’s time as Emperor ends.
The newest coins found on the Wall are made.

questions.prompt: Match each number to what it tells you about the Wall.
questions.explanation: These numbers are in lines 4, 6 and 12. Read the words next to a number to see what it counts.
pairs: the forts added before the work was finished

questions.prompt: The Wall is 73 miles long. The western 30 miles were built of turf. How many miles were not built of turf?
questions.explanation: 73 take away 30 is 43. These 43 miles are the stone part, which line 10 says was most of the Wall.

questions.prompt: “People from all these places met there and traded with each other” (line 14). What does this tell you about life on the Wall?
questions.explanation: Soldiers came from many places, and trading means buying and selling. So people from different lands met and did business.
options: It was a busy place where people from different lands mixed.
Nobody was allowed to buy or sell things.
Only Romans from Rome lived there.

questions.prompt: Ellie thinks the Wall was built in a few months by a small group of builders. Use the leaflet to explain why Ellie is wrong.
questions.explanation: This is a spot-the-mistake question. Check each part of what Ellie says against the leaflet.
questions.model: Ellie is wrong because “The work took at least 6 years” (line 6), not a few months. It was not a small group either: the Wall “was built by the 3 legions in Britain” and each legion had about 5,000 soldiers.
checklist: 1 mark: the work took at least 6 years.
1 mark: it was built by 3 legions, with about 5,000 soldiers in each.
Both parts of Ellie’s mistake must be corrected for 2 marks.
